method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar is near a three-week low because US government bond yields have fallen after last week's slide in tech shares. Businesses are still growing and raising prices, so a December Federal Reserve hike remains likely; the Fed decides on Wednesday, October 28, and what Chair Kevin Warsh says about December matters more than the decision itself.

EUR.text: The euro is steady near $1.12. Moody's surprised by not cutting France's credit rating late Friday, and German firms grew more hopeful in October, but France's budget fight and street protests continue and euro-area growth is slow. The European Central Bank is expected to hold on Thursday, October 29.

GBP.text: The pound is at its strongest against the euro since May 2025 after UK businesses had their best month since February, which makes a Bank of England hike on November 5 look close to certain. But shop sales fell in September and consumer confidence dropped the most since 2020, so households are feeling the squeeze before the October 28 budget.

JPY.text: The yen is near its strongest in a month, just under 157 per dollar, helped by lower US bond yields and signs that the Bank of Japan is moving closer to a rate hike. Oil easing on Gulf talks takes a little shelter demand away; the Bank of Japan decides on Friday, October 30, and is expected to hold.

CHF.text: The franc is near a three-month high against the euro as France's debt worries and falling shares sent money to shelter last week. The Swiss National Bank says it no longer needs to stand extra ready to stop the franc rising; a quiet weekend in the Gulf takes a little shelter demand away.

CAD.text: Most economists expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates to 2.50% on Wednesday, October 28, which supports the loonie near its strongest in a month. Oil easing on Monday is a small drag, and Friday's US tariff changes on Canadian goods were a minor reshuffle.

AUD.text: Australian business activity shrank in October for the first time in five months, and falling Asian shares add to the pressure. Rising costs keep a Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3 possible; inflation figures on October 28 should decide it.

NZD.text: The kiwi sits near 57 US cents as markets expect the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise its rate to 3.0% on Wednesday, October 28. Because the hike is expected, the bank's hints about further moves will matter more than the move itself.

XAU.text: Gold is just under $4,000, about a quarter below its January record. High oil keeps US rate hikes likely, gold pays no interest, and easing Gulf tensions on Monday take away some demand for shelter.

OIL.text: Brent oil fell to about $115 on Monday, more than 1% down, after a weekend without a US strike on Iran and as Qatari mediators met Iran's leaders. The supply risks remain: Yemen's Houthi rebels claim new strikes on Saudi Arabia's main oil pipeline, though Saudi Arabia has not confirmed damage.

items.headline: Germany Ifo business confidence improves in October as expectations surprise higher
items.story_title: Euro area: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: German firms grew more upbeat about the months ahead in October, even though they judged business today a little worse. It is the fifth monthly rise in the Ifo survey of German business mood.

beats.was: The Ifo index asks about 9,000 German companies how business is going now and how they expect it to go over the next six months. Germany is the euro area's biggest economy, and last week's euro-area business surveys showed growth slowing to a four-month low.
beats.happened: The overall reading edged up to 90.2 from 89.9, just above the 90.0 forecast. Hopes for the coming months jumped to their highest since February 2022, while firms' view of current conditions slipped below forecast.
beats.means: German companies expect better times ahead, but today's business is not improving yet, and surveys are not hard data. It softens last week's gloomy euro-area picture without changing it.
beats.fx: Brighter German outlook → slightly less worry about euro-area growth → a small help for the euro. It is unlikely to change the European Central Bank's decision on Thursday, October 29, where a hold is expected. The question to keep asking: is the euro area's slowdown bottoming out?

impact.why: Firms' hopes for the months ahead rose more than expected, though current business weakened.

items.watch: Whether hard data, like factory orders and output, start to follow the brighter outlook.

items.headline: Houthis say they attacked East-West oil pumping stations
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels said they hit pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's main cross-country oil pipeline and Riyadh's airport. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed it, and the Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed two Houthi missile launchers in Sanaa.

beats.was: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have been firing missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil sites, which helped push oil to a six-month high last week. The East-West pipeline carries Saudi crude to the Red Sea, letting it avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: The Houthis claimed new strikes on the pipeline's pumping stations and on Riyadh airport, after warning on Saturday that the airport remains a target. There was no Saudi confirmation of damage. The coalition said it intercepted a missile fired at Riyadh and destroyed the launcher.
beats.means: If the pipeline were damaged, Saudi Arabia would lose its main way around Hormuz. For now these are claims only, and oil fell on Monday anyway, so the market is treating them as contained.
beats.fx: Unconfirmed claims → limited extra supply fear → little lift for oil or the yen today. A confirmed hit would change that fast. The question to keep asking: is Saudi oil actually being disrupted?

impact.why: A hit on the pipeline would matter, but the claims are unconfirmed.
More fighting in the Gulf can send money to the yen for safety.

items.watch: Saudi confirmation or denial of damage to the East-West pipeline.

items.headline: Currency markets subdued ahead of pivotal central bank week
items.story_title: Five central banks decide this week
items.summary: Currencies barely moved on Monday as traders waited for five central-bank decisions this week. The Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan are expected to hold; Canada and New Zealand may raise rates.

beats.was: Oil above $110 has kept inflation high this year, so most central banks are leaning toward raising rates. Last week a slide in US tech shares sent money into US government bonds, pulling yields down and the dollar near a three-week low.
beats.happened: The euro sat near $1.12, the pound near $1.34 and the yen near 157 per dollar, all within a fraction of Friday. Oil eased after Qatari mediators went to Tehran. The Federal Reserve decides on Wednesday, October 28, along with the Bank of Canada and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand; the European Central Bank follows on Thursday and the Bank of Japan on Friday.
beats.means: The decisions themselves are mostly expected, so what each bank says about its next meetings will matter more. US interest rates have been setting the dollar's direction lately, and the gap between US rates and others has been narrowing.
beats.fx: Smaller rate gap between the US and others → less reason to hold dollars → a mild drag on the dollar. Canada and New Zealand hiking would support their currencies only if they signal more to come. The question to keep asking: who sounds readier to raise rates again?

impact.why: Lower US yields weigh, but a December Fed hike is still largely expected.
Markets expect a Bank of Canada hike on Wednesday.
Markets expect a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on Wednesday.

items.watch: What Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says about December at Wednesday's press conference (1:30 PM CT).

items.headline: Oil drops from near six-month highs on hopes Iran war hostilities to ease
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Oil fell more than 1% on Monday, with Brent near $115, after Qatari mediators went to Tehran with US backing and the weekend passed without a US strike on Iran.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea is still disrupted. Brent rose about 6% last week, to its highest in six months, as Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked Saudi oil sites, and a US envoy warned a strike on Iran could come over the weekend.
beats.happened: No strike came. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Sunday in a push to calm tensions, coordinated with the US, and officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were due to meet Iran's leaders on Monday. Brent fell about $1.50 to around $115.
beats.means: Some of the fear that drove last week's jump is fading, but the supply risks are still there. Analysts quoted say the relief may not last, and the head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, expects energy markets to stay disrupted through 2027.
beats.fx: Talks instead of strikes → less fear of a supply cut → oil eases → less need for shelter, so a little less support for the yen, and a small drag on the oil-linked Canadian dollar. The question to keep asking: is the Gulf heading toward talks or more fighting?

impact.why: Mediation in Tehran and a quiet weekend took some of the war fear out of the price.
Less war fear means less buying of the yen for safety.
Cheaper oil trims Canada's export income.

items.watch: Any outcome from Monday's Tehran meetings, or a new Houthi strike on Saudi oil.

items.headline: Japanese Yen holds near one-month top vs weak USD as traders await Fed, BoJ meetings
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: The yen held near its strongest in a month, just under 157 per dollar, ahead of the Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of Japan on Friday.

beats.was: The yen had been weak for months because Japan's interest rates are far below US rates. Last week it gained as falling shares and war worries sent money to shelter, and the dollar touched about 156, its lowest against the yen since mid-September.
beats.happened: The dollar's small bounce stalled below 157 yen. Lower US bond yields are holding the dollar back, while Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda has recently said underlying inflation is nearing the bank's 2% goal, a sign a rate hike is getting closer.
beats.means: The gap between US and Japanese interest rates may be starting to narrow from both sides: US yields have eased and Japan is edging toward a hike. Friday's Bank of Japan meeting is expected to keep rates at 1.25%, so its hints about the next move matter most.
beats.fx: Narrower US–Japan rate gap → less reward for borrowing in yen to buy dollars → support for the yen. The question to keep asking: how close is the Bank of Japan to its next hike?

impact.why: Lower US yields and hints of a Bank of Japan hike support the yen.
Falling US bond yields limit the dollar's bounce.

items.watch: Bank of Japan decision and Governor Ueda's comments on Friday, October 30.

items.headline: Hundreds of thousands protest in France amid heightened police security
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: About 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, by the government's count, over school conditions and living costs. Marches were mostly peaceful, with about 1,000 arrests, fewer than the week before.

beats.was: Protests over run-down schools, teacher shortages and the cost of living turned into looting and violence a week earlier, adding to worries about France's budget and debt.
beats.happened: The Interior Ministry counted 410,000 marchers, 110,000 of them in Paris; unions said about twice that. More than 70,000 police were deployed and several marches were banned or moved. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests, against more than 2,000 after the October 17 protests.
beats.means: Calmer than the week before, but students say they will keep marching until they see action. Ongoing unrest makes it harder for the government to pass spending cuts.
beats.fx: Lasting unrest → harder to cut the deficit → investors want more to hold French debt → a mild drag on the euro. The question to keep asking: is the unrest fading or spreading?

impact.why: Unrest makes a deficit-cutting budget harder, though this weekend was calmer.

items.watch: Whether students and unions call more marches, and how parliament votes on the budget.

items.headline: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Further Modifies Canadian Products Subject to Tariffs Under Section 338
items.story_title: US–Canada: tariff changes
items.summary: President Trump changed which Canadian goods face US tariffs: plywood, some paper, some machinery and packing crates come off the list, while some valves, carpets and waste products go on. The changes start October 30.

beats.was: The US has put tariffs on a list of Canadian goods after trade talks broke down and Canada hit back with tariffs on about $20 billion of US exports.
beats.happened: Trump signed an order swapping some products on and off the list. Earlier reports had said farm and forestry goods would get relief; the final list is mostly industrial goods, and narrower than reported.
beats.means: It is a reshuffle, not a broad easing. The overall trade fight between the US and Canada is unchanged.
beats.fx: Small, mixed tariff change → little change to Canada's export outlook → little effect on the loonie, which is being driven more by oil and Wednesday's expected Bank of Canada hike. The question to keep asking: is the US–Canada trade fight easing or widening?

impact.why: Some goods get relief and others are added, so the net effect is small.

items.watch: Any sign of wider US–Canada trade talks restarting.

items.headline: US could strike Iran as soon as this weekend, says US ambassador Tom Barrack
items.story_title: US–Iran: talks or new strikes?
items.summary: Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey, said a US strike on Iran could come this weekend, cutting against President Trump's earlier word that nothing would happen before the November 3 midterm elections.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. A truce agreed in June has mostly broken down, Iran has been blocking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and President Trump had said new strikes would not come before the US midterm elections on November 3.
beats.happened: Speaking on a podcast while visiting the Gulf, Barrack said a strike 'this weekend' was possible, though he added the US is still open to a deal and is not seeking to overthrow Iran's government. He has no direct role on Iran. Earlier Friday, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, told the Financial Times the war could last another year, and Iranian state TV said ships that don't follow Iran's rules can no longer pass through Hormuz.
beats.means: It is one official's comment, not an announced plan, but it brings the risk of a new round of fighting forward into the weekend, when markets are closed and can't react.
beats.fx: Fear of a weekend strike → investors cut risk before the close and buy oil and shelter → helps oil, the yen and the franc; hurts the euro and currencies tied to global growth.

impact.why: A strike would threaten Gulf supply, but this is an unconfirmed comment from an envoy without an Iran role.
Investors tend to buy the yen when war risk rises.
The franc is the other usual place to shelter.
The Aussie tends to fall when investors pull back from risk.

items.watch: Any word from the White House on timing, and how oil opens on Sunday evening.

items.headline: Brent oil jumps 3.5% to about $117, its highest since late April, as attacks on tankers pick up
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Brent oil climbed about $4 to near $117 by midday in New York on Friday, heading for a weekly gain of nearly 7%, as attacks on Gulf tankers and Saudi Arabia kept piling up.

beats.was: Oil has been rising for three weeks as Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, strike Saudi Arabia, and Iran harasses ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's main shipping lane. Brent was under $97 at the start of October.
beats.happened: Brent rose to about $117.2 a barrel and US crude to about $103. A Washington think tank says October is the worst month on record for attacks on ships in and around Hormuz. Analysts linked the UAE oil spill to a tanker hit by a projectile on October 9, and a shut valve is cutting output at two Libyan oilfields. An independent oil consultant said more oil is leaving Hormuz lately, but that could reverse at any moment.
beats.means: The rise sped up through Friday, so this is no longer just the same worry already in the price: buyers are paying more each day to secure barrels as the attacks spread.
beats.fx: Dearer oil → more income for Canada and Norway, bigger import bills for Japan and the euro area, and higher inflation worries everywhere → helps the loonie, weighs on the yen and euro, and keeps central banks leaning toward hikes.

impact.why: A fast $4 jump to the highest since April, on a growing list of attacks on ships and Saudi sites.
Canada sells oil abroad, so a dearer barrel adds to its income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so its bill rises.
The euro area buys most of its energy abroad and its economy is already slowing.

items.watch: Whether Brent holds above $115 into Friday's close, and whether any attack actually cuts Saudi or Gulf exports.

items.headline: Brent oil tops $115, its highest since early May, on Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia and a tanker spill off the UAE
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Brent oil rose about 1.5% to near $115 on Friday, its highest since May 4, as fighting in Saudi Arabia went on and the UAE reported oil leaking from a tanker off its coast.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, have been attacking Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, since moving toward the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb strait last month. On Thursday Saudi Aramco, the state oil company, cleared its Dhahran headquarters.
beats.happened: Brent touched $115.16 a barrel and is heading for a third weekly rise of about 4%. US crude rose to about $101. The UAE's environment ministry reported an oil spill from an unnamed tanker off Umm Al Quwain without giving a cause, and a shut pipeline valve in Libya is cutting output there. A UBS analyst said high shipping costs and uneven oil flows have left the market short of supply.
beats.means: Each new incident adds to the worry that the Gulf's oil can't move freely, so prices keep climbing even without a confirmed cut to Saudi exports.
beats.fx: Dearer oil → more income for Canada, higher import bills for Japan and the euro area → helps the loonie, weighs on the yen and euro.

impact.why: A new five-month high, but driven by the same Saudi fighting that is already in the price.
Canada earns more when oil is dear.
Japan buys nearly all its oil abroad, so a dearer barrel costs it more.

items.watch: Whether the UAE names the tanker or a cause for the spill, and whether any attack actually stops Saudi oil leaving port.

items.headline: US consumer mood revised up to 48.0 in October, still near record lows
items.summary: The University of Michigan's final October survey shows Americans a bit less gloomy than first estimated, but still among the most downbeat on record. They expect prices to keep rising fast.

beats.was: US consumer confidence fell to a record low in May after the war with Iran sent fuel prices soaring, and has stayed weak since. The Fed watches the survey's inflation expectations closely.
beats.happened: The University of Michigan's final consumer sentiment reading for October came in at 48.0, above the 46.3 first estimate. Views of current conditions worsened, while hopes for the months ahead improved. Households expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year and 3.5% a year over five to ten years.
beats.means: Americans feel squeezed by living costs ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, but this has not yet shown up as a collapse in spending. High price expectations are the part that worries the Fed.
beats.fx: Gloomy but not collapsing, with high price expectations → little change to Fed hike bets → small effect on the dollar.

impact.why: Weak mood is a drag, but sticky inflation expectations keep the Fed alert; markets barely moved.

items.watch: The Conference Board's consumer confidence survey on October 27, the day before the Fed decision.
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: hold on October 28, hike in December?

items.headline: US business growth cools in October, but firms raise prices at the fastest pace since 2022
items.summary: S&P Global's early October survey shows US business activity still growing fast, if a little slower than September's five-year high. Orders are strong and companies are passing on higher costs.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised its main rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September as oil prices, pushed up by the US-Israeli war with Iran, lifted inflation. It meets again on October 27-28.
beats.happened: S&P Global's flash survey of US purchasing managers fell to 57.6 in October from 58.4; anything above 50 means growth. New orders were the highest since March 2022, and the prices firms charge rose at the quickest pace since August 2022. Factories hired at the fastest rate since 2012.
beats.means: Demand in the US is holding up well despite dear fuel, and businesses are able to pass costs on to customers. That keeps inflation pressure alive and the Fed leaning toward another hike.
beats.fx: Strong demand and rising prices → keeps a December Fed hike on the table → supports the dollar.

impact.why: Solid growth and faster price rises back the case for a December Fed hike, but the reading was close to forecasts.

items.watch: The first estimate of US third-quarter growth next week, and the Fed's decision on October 28.
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: hold on October 28, hike in December?

items.headline: Canada August retail sales +1.2% vs +1.3% expected
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: an October 28 rate hike?
items.summary: Canadian shop sales bounced back 1.2% in August after falling in July, and an early estimate says they rose again in September. The loonie firmed past 1.40 per US dollar.

beats.was: Canadian shoppers cut back in July, the first monthly fall in sales in seven months. The Bank of Canada decides on October 28 whether to raise interest rates to fight rising prices.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada said retail sales rose 1.2% in August, just under the 1.3% forecast. Leaving out car dealers, sales also rose 1.2%, more than the 1.0% expected. Its early estimate for September points to a further 0.7% gain. The US dollar slipped below 1.40 Canadian dollars.
beats.means: Canadian households are still spending despite dearer fuel and higher borrowing costs, which gives the central bank room to raise rates next week.
beats.fx: Shoppers still spending → more room for a Bank of Canada hike → supports the loonie.

impact.why: Strong spending in August and September backs the case for an October 28 rate hike.

items.watch: Canada's September inflation figures and how much of a hike markets price before October 28.

items.headline: Oil prices rise as Houthis launch another wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: Brent oil climbed to about $114.50 on Friday after Yemen's Houthi rebels said they struck more Saudi targets, including an Aramco site at the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, have spent the week attacking Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter. Saudi Aramco, the state oil company, has already cleared its Dhahran headquarters.
beats.happened: The Houthis said that over two days they hit the Saudi defence ministry in Riyadh, airports in Dammam and Abha, and an Aramco site at Yanbu that includes an oil loading port. Two people died at Dammam airport. Brent rose about 1% to near $114.50, set for a third weekly gain, and US crude rose to about $100.80. A shut pipeline valve in Libya is also cutting output there.
beats.means: Yanbu is the port Saudi Arabia uses to ship oil out by the Red Sea, away from the Gulf, so attacks there go straight at its backup export route.
beats.fx: Saudi export route under fire → oil higher → helps oil sellers like Canada, weighs on big buyers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Fresh strikes on a Saudi export port and airports push Brent to a new five-month high.
Canada earns more when oil is dear.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a dearer barrel costs it more.

items.watch: Whether any strike actually cuts Saudi exports from Yanbu, or the attacks ease.

items.headline: Euro heads for a weekly loss against the dollar and yen as France's debt worries return
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: The euro slipped to about $1.12 and fell to its weakest against the yen since October 2025, as France's borrowing costs rose again and euro-area business growth slowed.

beats.was: France is fighting over its budget amid street protests, and investors now demand the most extra interest to lend to France instead of Germany since the euro debt crisis of 2011. The European Central Bank (ECB) meets on October 29.
beats.happened: The euro was set for a weekly fall of about 0.4% against the dollar, 1.2% against the yen and 0.5% against the Swiss franc, touching 175.4 yen. October business surveys showed euro-area growth at a four-month low, with France shrinking. A Citi economist said France is a drag but the rest of the euro area is holding up; a Commerzbank strategist said the euro is frozen until next week's central bank meetings.
beats.means: France's debt troubles are now pulling on the whole euro, and the slowdown gives the ECB a reason to be careful about hiking.
beats.fx: Rising French borrowing costs and slower growth → less appetite for euro assets and a more cautious ECB → weighs on the euro, most clearly against the yen and franc.

impact.why: A modest weekly loss on France worries and weak surveys that were already known.
Investors are using the yen as shelter from France and falling shares.
The franc also gains when the euro is under strain.

items.watch: Moody's verdict on France's credit rating, due after Friday's US close, and the ECB on October 29.

items.headline: France spared Moody's ratings downgrade as it struggles with unrest
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: Moody's kept France's credit rating at Aa3 late Friday, with a negative outlook, when bond markets had expected a downgrade. It is a reprieve, not an all-clear.

beats.was: France is struggling to pass a budget that cuts its deficit, and protests over schools and living costs turned violent last week. Its 10-year borrowing cost hit about 5.1%, the highest since 2002, and the extra it pays over Germany was the most in 15 years. S&P and Fitch had already cut France's rating.
beats.happened: Moody's left France's rating unchanged after markets closed on Friday, instead of the expected one-step cut. It is counting on a deficit-cutting 2027 budget being passed and said getting past the split parliament is what will decide its next move.
beats.means: Avoiding a downgrade takes some immediate pressure off French bonds. But the warning stays, the budget can still fail in parliament, and the 2027 presidential election is a further risk.
beats.fx: No downgrade → less forced selling of French bonds → a small relief for the euro. The question to keep asking: can France pass a budget that cuts its deficit?

impact.why: Markets had priced a downgrade that did not come, easing pressure on French bonds.

items.watch: Votes on France's 2027 budget and any no-confidence motion against the government.

items.headline: Most economists in a Reuters poll now expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates to 2.50% on October 28
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: an October 28 rate hike?
items.summary: A slim majority of economists now expect the Bank of Canada to raise its rate by a quarter point next week, its first move in a year, and many see one more hike by March.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada's rate has been 2.25% for a year, and a month ago most economists expected it to stay there through 2026. Since then Canadian inflation rose to 3.1% in September and oil prices soared.
beats.happened: In a Reuters poll taken October 21-23, 19 of 34 economists expect a hike to 2.50% on October 28, and 16 of 29 expect another to 2.75% by the end of March. They pointed to the September inflation figure, a central-bank survey showing businesses expect faster price rises, broken-down trade talks with the US, and recent hints from Governor Tiff Macklem. Markets now put the odds of an October hike at about three in four, up from roughly 30%.
beats.means: Forecasters have caught up with markets: a hike is now the expected outcome, though a sizable minority still thinks the weak economy will hold the bank back.
beats.fx: A likely hike plus more to come → higher Canadian rates → support for the loonie, though much of it is already priced.

impact.why: Economists now back the hike markets were already expecting.

items.watch: The Bank of Canada's decision and statement on October 28, and whether it signals more than one hike.

items.headline: UK retail sales fall by more than expected in September
items.story_title: UK: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: British shops sold less in September than forecast, as a warm start to autumn kept people from buying winter clothes and dearer fuel squeezed budgets.

beats.was: UK shop sales had grown over the summer, helped by the World Cup and a heatwave, and a separate survey this week showed consumer confidence falling sharply in October.
beats.happened: Sales volumes fell 0.4% in September, worse than the 0.1% dip economists expected, according to the Office for National Statistics. Over the three months to September they still rose 0.7%, and July and August were revised up.
beats.means: Households are spending more on fuel and less elsewhere, a sign that high energy prices are starting to bite ahead of the October 28 budget.
beats.fx: Softer spending → small doubt over how far the Bank of England can raise rates → mild weight on the pound.

impact.why: A modest miss with good summer revisions, overshadowed by the strong business survey.

items.watch: October retail figures and whether the budget eases or tightens household finances.

items.headline: Yen shines as AI jitters spur safe-haven rush
items.story_title: Shelter buying: yen and franc
items.summary: The yen reached its strongest in over a month, near 156.3 per dollar, and is heading for its best week since early September as nervous investors look for shelter.

beats.was: The yen and the Swiss franc usually gain when investors get scared, and this week brought a slide in US tech shares, Gulf attacks and worries about France's debt.
beats.happened: On Friday the yen rose 0.3% to about 156.3 per dollar, on track for a 1% weekly gain. The dollar index was near its lowest since early October, the franc held near a one-month high, and the Canadian dollar firmed past 1.40 per US dollar. Japan's core inflation also rose above the Bank of Japan's 2% goal for the first time in nine months.
beats.means: Each worry is helping a different shelter: AI fears the yen, France's troubles the franc, and dearer oil the Canadian dollar.
beats.fx: Risk worries + firmer Japanese inflation → more demand for the yen; oil above $110 → supports the loonie.

impact.why: Shelter buying and a firmer case for a Bank of Japan hike, extending this week's gain.
France's debt worries keep money flowing to the franc.
High oil prices keep the loonie near a one-month high.

items.watch: Whether the Bank of Japan, meeting October 29–30, hints at a December hike; most economists polled by Reuters expect a hold next week.

items.headline: UK consumer confidence tumbles ahead of Healey's budget, GfK reports
items.story_title: UK: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: British shoppers' mood fell in October by the most since the start of the pandemic, with fewer planning big purchases and more expecting higher prices.

beats.was: In September GfK's monthly UK consumer confidence index had reached -13, its best level in over two years, and the Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5.
beats.happened: The index fell 11 points to -24 in October, worse than every forecast in a Reuters poll and the steepest monthly drop since April 2020. GfK pointed to rising prices, the Middle East war and tighter household budgets; people's inflation expectations rose too.
beats.means: Households are pulling back just as rates look set to rise, which raises the risk that the UK economy slows and limits how far the Bank of England can go.
beats.fx: Weaker consumer demand → doubts about a long run of UK rate hikes → weighs on the pound.

impact.why: A far bigger fall in confidence than expected, days before the October 28 budget.
